title: Reporting Ongoing Work: "We've Been Working On…"
titleEs: Informar del trabajo en curso: «We've been working on…»
summary: Report work in progress to a colleague: the Present Perfect Continuous for the activity (*we've been working on it since March*) and the Present Perfect Simple for the results (*we've migrated three modules so far*).
canDo: Report an activity that is still in progress with *have been + -ing* and *since / for*.
Give results so far with *have + past participle*, *so far* and numbers.
Ask for a status update with *How long…?* and *How many…?*
Link consonant to vowel in *work on it* and *roll it out*, and say *been* as a weak /bɪn/.

focus.grammar: Present Perfect Continuous (activity, duration: since / for) vs Present Perfect Simple (result: so far, yet, quantity) · How long…? vs How many…? · stative verbs
focus.lexis: work on, so far, be on track, a blocker, up and running, narrow something down to, keep someone posted, loop someone in, plug away at, remain pending, have now been completed
focus.afh: linking in work on it / roll it out · weak been /bɪn/ · schedule US /sk/ vs UK /ʃ/ · PROgress (n.) vs proGRESS (v.)

warmup: Think of something you have been working on for a while: a project, a course, a move. What have you finished so far, and what is still open? Say one sentence about each.

scenario.title: Welcome back: where we are
scenario.context: Ryan coordinates the migration of his company's customer portal to a new platform. Oliver, his colleague, has been on leave for two weeks and comes back tomorrow. Ryan sends him a voice message on Sunday evening.
scenario.speaker: ryan
scenario.text: Hi Oliver, welcome back! Quick update before tomorrow's stand-up so you're not lost. We{{'ve been working on}} the portal migration non-stop since you left. {{So far}}, we{{'ve migrated}} three of the five modules, and Priya {{has been testing}} the new design with real users for two weeks now. The reporting module is {{still pending}}: Alex has been chasing a bug in the data export, and we haven't found the cause yet. Overall, we're {{on track}} for the June rollout. I'll {{loop you in}} on the client call on Wednesday. See you tomorrow!

dialogue.title: Monday stand-up
dialogue.context: Oliver is back. Ryan runs the team's short Monday meeting with Priya (UX designer) and Alex (developer).

lines.text: Morning, everyone. Oliver's back, so let's do a proper round. Priya, where are we with the user testing?

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Good, actually. I{{'ve been running}} sessions with real customers for two weeks, and we{{'ve completed}} twelve of the fifteen interviews. The main finding {{so far}}: people can't find the invoices page.

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: Noted. Alex, what about the data export bug?

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: I{{'ve been digging into}} it since Thursday. I{{'ve narrowed it down}} to the date format, but I haven't fixed it yet. I should have a fix by tomorrow.

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: Is that {{the blocker}} for the reporting module?

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: It is. Everything else in that module is {{up and running}}.

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: Okay. And {{how long has}} the client {{been waiting}} for the demo?

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: Since the end of April. Helen has been asking for a date, so let's agree on one today and I'll {{keep her posted}}.

comprehension.q: How long has Priya been running sessions with customers?
comprehension.explain: *I've been running sessions with real customers for two weeks.* Activity in progress + *for* + length of time.

comprehension.q: What has Alex found out about the bug so far?
options: He has narrowed it down to the date format.
He hasn't started looking at it yet.
comprehension.explain: *I've narrowed it down to the date format, but I haven't fixed it yet.* A result so far (simple), then what is still open (*yet*).

comprehension.q: Why does Ryan want to agree on a demo date today?
options: Because Oliver is back from leave.
Because Helen has been asking for a date since the end of April.
Because the reporting module is finished.
comprehension.explain: *Helen has been asking for a date*: the client has been waiting since the end of April.

discovery.intro: Ryan sums up the project. Two forms share the same auxiliary *have*, but they point at different things: the work itself, or what the work has produced.
discovery.speaker: ryan
discovery.text: We{{'ve been working on}} the portal migration since March. So far, we{{'ve migrated}} three of the five modules, and Priya {{has been testing}} the new design with real users for two weeks. We {{haven't finished}} the reporting module yet, but we're on track.

organizer.title: Activity or result?
organizer.prompt: Complete the table with the missing form or focus. Type the pattern, not the whole sentence.
rows: We{{'ve been working on}} the migration since March.
the activity: still going on, how long
We{{'ve migrated}} three of the five modules.
Priya {{has been testing}} the design for two weeks.

accept: the activity: still going on, how long

rows: We {{haven't finished}} the reporting module yet.
organizer.explain: Continuous = activity and duration (*since / for*); simple = result and quantity (*so far*, numbers). *Yet* goes with the negative simple.

questions.q: Compare *we've been working on the migration since March* and *we've migrated three of the five modules*. Which one describes an activity that is still going on, and which one a finished result? Say how you know: look at the time words and at what comes after the verb.
questions.model: *We've been working on the migration since March* is an activity that started in the past and is still going on: *since March* gives the starting point, and the migration is not finished. *We've migrated three of the five modules* is a finished result: a number of things completed up to now, which is why *so far* goes with it. The continuous looks at the work; the simple counts what the work has produced.
criteria: You said the continuous form (*have been working*) describes an activity that is still in progress.
You said the simple form (*have migrated*) describes a completed result.
You used the clues: *since March* / *for two weeks* with the continuous, *so far* and a number with the simple.

questions.q: How is each form built? Write both patterns (the auxiliaries and the form of the main verb), and say which time expressions go with each one: *since March*, *for two weeks*, *so far*, *yet*.
questions.model: Continuous: *have / has + been + verb-ing* (*we've been working*, *she has been testing*). It takes *since* + a starting point and *for* + a length of time. Simple: *have / has + past participle* (*we've migrated*, *we haven't finished*). It takes *so far*, *already*, *yet* in negatives and questions, and a quantity (*three of the five modules*).
criteria: You wrote the continuous pattern: *have / has been + -ing*.
You wrote the simple pattern: *have / has + past participle*.
You matched *since / for* with the continuous and *so far / yet* (and quantities) with the simple.

questions.q: Ryan says *we've been working on it since March*, not *we worked on it in March* or *we've done the migration*. What does the continuous form tell Helen, the client, about the team's effort and about the present? And when would a manager deliberately choose the simple form instead?
questions.model: The continuous highlights sustained effort and duration (*how long*), and it makes clear that the work is not finished: a fair picture of an ongoing project, and a polite way of saying *we're still on it*. A manager chooses the simple form to show results and evidence (*we've migrated three modules*, *we've completed twelve interviews*): numbers reassure a client more than effort does, so a good status update combines both.
criteria: You said the continuous emphasises effort and duration (*how long*).
You said it signals that the work is still unfinished (a diplomatic *we're still on it*).
You said the simple form is chosen to show results, numbers or evidence.

points: Present Perfect Continuous (*have / has been + -ing*) describes an activity that started in the past and is still going on. It answers *How long?*: *since* + starting point, *for* + length of time.

Present Perfect Simple (*have / has + past participle*) describes a result that is complete now. It answers *How many? What have you done?*: *so far*, *already*, a quantity, and *yet* in negatives and questions.
A good status update needs both: the activity first (*We've been working on the migration since March*), then the evidence (*So far, we've migrated three modules*).
Stative verbs (*know, have, need, be, own, believe*) stay in the simple form even for duration: *We've known about the bug since Monday*, never *We've been knowing*.
formulas: have / has been + verb-ing + since / for
have / has + past participle + so far / already / yet
How long have you been + -ing? · How many have you + past participle?
rule.note: Spanish says *llevamos tres meses trabajando* or *trabajamos en esto desde marzo* with a present tense. English needs the perfect: *We've been working on it for three months / since March*. Never *We are working on it since March*.

phonetics.intro: Las frases de estado se dicen en bloques, no palabra por palabra: *work on it*, *roll it out*, *keep an eye on*. El hispanohablante tiende a separar cada palabra, a pronunciar *been* con vocal larga y a meter una /e/ en *schedule*. Aquí enlazamos consonante con vocal, debilitamos *been* y fijamos el acento de *progress*.

items.meaning: to spend time trying to finish or improve it

alerts.text: La k de *work* se une a *on* («uér-kon») y la n de *on* se une a *it* («ko-nit»). Tres palabras, un solo bloque: «UÉR-ka-nit». Si paras entre palabras, suena robótico.
*Work* lleva la vocal con r /ɝ/ (US): ni «uork» ni «guork». No añadas una g delante de la u.
La k final de *work* no se pierde: es justo la que enlaza con *on*.

example.speaker: alex
example.text: I'll work on it this afternoon and send you the results.

items.meaning: past participle of be; in have been + -ing it is unstressed
items.say: Been. We've been working on it.

alerts.text: En *we've been working*, *been* es átono y corto: /bɪn/, «bin», como *bin* (cubo). No digas «biiin». En Reino Unido se oye más /biːn/, pero también breve.
/ɪ/ es una i relajada, entre la i y la e españolas. Compárala con *seen* /siːn/, que sí es larga.
*We've been* se dice de un tirón: la v de *we've* pasa directamente a *been*: «uiv-bin».

example.speaker: ryan
example.text: We've been testing the new design for two weeks.
example.tts: We've [been](/bɪn/) testing the new design for two weeks.

items.meaning: to make a new product or system available to users, in stages

alerts.text: La l de *roll* se une a *out*: «ro-LAUT», no «rol / aut». Con *it* en medio: «ro-li-RAUT».
En inglés americano, la t de *it* queda entre vocales y suena como una r suave española: «ro-li-RAUT». En británico se oye la t: «ro-li-TAUT».
La r inicial de *roll* no vibra como la rr española: la lengua no toca el paladar.

example.speaker: alex
example.text: We're going to roll it out to the first fifty users on Monday.

items.meaning: a plan that says when things will happen; on schedule = on time

alerts.text: Empieza con /sk/, sin e de apoyo: «sss-KE-dyul», nunca «es-KE-dyul».
En Reino Unido se oye sobre todo «SHE-dyul» /ˈʃedʒ.uːl/. Las dos formas se entienden en todas partes; elige una y mantenla.
Acento en la primera sílaba. La segunda es breve: «dyul», con /dʒ/ («dy»), no «dul».

example.speaker: daniel
example.text: The server upgrade is still on schedule for Friday.

variants.label: Noun: PRO-gress
variants.speaker: coach
variants.text: We've made good progress this month.

alerts.text: Sustantivo: acento en la primera sílaba, «PRA-gres» (*make progress*). Verbo: acento en la segunda, «pra-GRES» (*the work is progressing*). En español «progreso» siempre lleva el acento en GRE.
En EE. UU. la o del sustantivo es una a abierta /ɑː/: «PRA-gres». En Reino Unido es /əʊ/: «PRÓU-gres».
La *-ss* final es una s sorda /s/, igual que en español. No la hagas sonora.

example.speaker: priya
example.text: We've made a lot of progress on the new design this month.
example.tts: We've made a lot of [progress](/pɹˈɑɡɹɛs/) on the new design this month.

structures.title: Activity in progress: Present Perfect Continuous
structures.formula: Subject + have / has + been + verb-ing (+ since / for)
structures.usage: For work that started in the past and is still going on. It stresses how long and how much effort, not whether the work is finished.

examples.speaker: coach
examples.text: We{{'ve been working on}} the migration since March.
examples.tts: We've [been](/bɪn/) working on the migration since March.

examples.speaker: priya
examples.text: I{{'ve been testing}} the new design for two weeks.

structures.title: Result up to now: Present Perfect Simple
structures.formula: Subject + have / has + past participle (+ so far / already / yet)
structures.usage: For what is finished at the moment of speaking: results, numbers, milestones. *Yet* in negatives and questions.

examples.speaker: coach
examples.text: So far, we{{'ve migrated}} three of the five modules.

examples.speaker: alex
examples.text: I{{'ve narrowed it down}} to the date format, but I {{haven't fixed}} it yet.

structures.title: Asking for status: How long…? and How many…?
structures.formula: How long + have / has + subject + been + -ing? · How many + noun + have / has + subject + past participle?
structures.usage: *How long* asks about the activity (continuous); *how many / how much* asks about the results (simple).

examples.speaker: oliver
examples.text: {{How long has}} the client {{been waiting}} for the demo?

l1.title: Present tense for an unfinished period
l1.text: Spanish uses the present (*llevamos tres meses trabajando*, *trabajamos en esto desde marzo*). English needs the Present Perfect Continuous: the activity started in the past.
l1.wrong: We are working on the migration since March.
l1.right: We've been working on the migration since March.

l1.title: Since with a length of time
l1.text: *Since* takes the starting point; *for* takes the duration. Spanish *desde hace tres semanas* covers both, which is why *since three weeks* appears.
l1.wrong: She has been testing the design since two weeks.
l1.right: She has been testing the design for two weeks.

l1.title: Continuous with a counted result
l1.text: If you count what is finished, use the simple form. The continuous describes the activity, not the number.
l1.wrong: We've been migrating three modules so far.
l1.right: We've migrated three modules so far.

l1.title: Stative verbs in the continuous
l1.text: *Know, need, have, be, own, believe* do not take the continuous, even with *since* or *for*.
l1.wrong: We've been knowing about the bug since Monday.
l1.right: We've known about the bug since Monday.

l1.title: Actually for «actualmente»
l1.text: *Actually* means *in fact*: a correction or a surprise. For the present moment, use *currently* or *at the moment*.
l1.wrong: Actually we are testing the design with real users.
l1.right: We're currently testing the design with real users.

practice.text: We ___ on the migration since March, and we're on track.
practice.explain: An activity still in progress with *since* → Present Perfect Continuous.

practice.text: So far, we ___ three of the five modules.
practice.explain: A finished quantity (*three modules*) with *so far* → Present Perfect Simple.

practice.text: Priya has been testing the design ___ two weeks.
practice.explain: A length of time → *for*. *Since* needs a starting point; *during* answers *when*, not *how long*.

practice.text: We ___ about the bug since Monday.
practice.explain: *Know* is a stative verb: no continuous. *Since* rules out the present simple.

practice.prompt: Complete with the correct form of *dig*.
practice.text: Alex has ___ into the bug since Thursday.
practice.explain: An activity in progress since a point in time → *has been digging*.

practice.prompt: Complete the question with one word.
practice.text: How ___ has the client been waiting for the demo?
practice.explain: *How long* asks about duration and goes with the continuous.

practice.prompt: Complete with the word that goes with a negative Present Perfect.
practice.text: We haven't fixed the date-format bug ___.
practice.explain: *Yet* = up to now, in negatives and questions.

practice.answer: We've been working on it since March
practice.explain: Continuous for an unfinished activity + *since* + starting point.

practice.answer: How many interviews have you completed so far
practice.explain: *How many* asks about results: Present Perfect Simple.

practice.wrong: We are working on the portal since March.
accept: We've been working on the portal since March.
We have been working on the portal since March.
practice.explain: *Since* + an unfinished activity → Present Perfect Continuous, not the present.

practice.wrong: She has been testing the design since two weeks.
accept: She has been testing the design for two weeks.
She's been testing the design for two weeks.

practice.wrong: Actually we are testing the design with real users.
accept: Currently we are testing the design with real users.
Currently, we are testing the design with real users.
We are currently testing the design with real users.
We're currently testing the design with real users.
At the moment we are testing the design with real users.
At the moment, we are testing the design with real users.
practice.explain: *Actually* = in fact. For the present moment: *currently* or *at the moment*.

practice.explain: **PRO**-gress as a noun; pro-**GRESS** as a verb.

practice.explain: A result with a number: Present Perfect Simple + *so far*.

task.title: A status update for a colleague back from leave
task.scenario: A colleague on your team has been away for two weeks and comes back tomorrow. Record (or write) a short voice message so that they are not lost at the stand-up: what the team has been doing, what is finished, what is still open and what happens next. Use a real or an imagined project you know well.
task.brief: Give an ongoing-work update: activity in progress, results so far, open issues and the next step.
steps: Open with a welcome and the purpose of the message.
Say what the team has been working on and since when (activity + duration).
Give two or three results so far, with numbers (finished work).
Name one issue that is still open and what someone has been doing about it.
Close with the overall status and the next step for your colleague.

chunks.label: status chunk
chunks.re: \b(on track|behind schedule|up and running|blocker|pending|workaround|loop you in|keep you posted)\b

extra.title: Extra: the formal status line
extra.brief: Rewrite your overall status as one formal sentence for the client's weekly report: an impersonal subject, the passive where it helps, no *we've been busy*.

parts.speaker: alex
parts.text: Hi Sarah, welcome back! Here's where we are with the help-center project. We{{'ve been rewriting}} the support articles since the start of May, and we're about halfway. {{So far}}, we{{'ve published}} forty of the eighty articles, and we{{'ve set up}} the new search. The video tutorials are {{still pending}}: Leo {{has been editing}} them for a week, but we {{haven't signed off}} on the first one {{yet}}, because the sound quality is {{a blocker}}. Overall, we're {{on track}} for the end of June. I'll {{keep you posted}} and {{loop you in}} on Thursday's review. See you tomorrow!
parts.tts: Hi Sarah, welcome back! Here's where we are with the help-center project. We've been rewriting the support articles since the start of May, and we're about halfway. So far, we've published forty of the eighty articles, and we've set up the new search. The video tutorials are still pending: Leo has been editing them for a week, but we haven't signed off on the first one yet, because the sound quality is a blocker. Overall, we're on track for the end of June. I'll keep you posted and loop you in on Thursday's review. See you tomorrow!
parts.label: Voice message to a colleague (neutral)
notes: *We've been rewriting… since the start of May*: the activity and its starting point come first.
*So far, we've published forty of the eighty articles*: results with numbers in the simple form.
*Still pending*, *hasn't… yet*, *a blocker*: what is open, without drama.
*Keep you posted* and *loop you in* close with a next step; the tone stays friendly (*welcome back*, *see you tomorrow*).

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{As of today}}, work on the help-center project {{has been progressing}} steadily: forty of the eighty articles {{have now been published}}, while the video tutorials {{remain pending}} until the sound issue {{has been resolved}}.
parts.label: Formal status line for the client's report (written)
notes: *As of today* dates the report. *Work on the project* is an impersonal subject: no *we've been busy*.
*Have now been published*, *has been resolved*: the passive keeps the focus on the work, not on people.
*Remain pending* replaces the conversational *still not done*.

selfCheck.text: ¿Tu mensaje transmite a la vez esfuerzo sostenido (continuo + *since / for*) y resultados concretos (simple + números)? Si solo hay esfuerzo, quien escucha no sabe qué está hecho; si solo hay resultados, no sabe cuánto ha costado.
¿El tono es el de un compañero (*welcome back*, *quick update*, *see you tomorrow*) y no el de un informe? ¿Y la frase extra suena a informe (sujeto impersonal, pasiva) y no a chat?
¿Escribiste *we are working… since* o *since two weeks*? En inglés: *we've been working… since March*, *for two weeks*.
¿Los verbos de estado (*know, need, have*) van en forma simple (*we've known about it since Monday*)? ¿Pusiste *yet* al final de las negativas?
Si te faltó una palabra técnica, ¿la rodeaste con una paráfrasis (*the thing that stops the export from working*) en lugar de pasar al español o dejar la frase a medias?
